title: Walmart Earnings Preview: What Analysts Expect Before the Bell – CNBC Insights
body:
Walmart Co. will unveil its third‑quarter fiscal results before the market opens on Thursday, offering the first concrete gauge of how U.S. shoppers are responding to a year‑long squeeze on disposable income. Analysts expect the retail giant to highlight a shift toward lower‑priced, convenience‑driven purchases as consumers brace for the holiday season, a trend that could reshape the competitive landscape for big‑box and online merchants alike.

The earnings release comes at a pivotal moment for the world’s largest retailer. After a year marked by elevated inflation, volatile gasoline prices and a tightening labor market, consumer confidence has slipped to its lowest level in more than a decade. Yet Walmart’s expansive footprint—spanning supercenters, neighborhood markets and a robust e‑commerce platform—positions it to capture demand from shoppers who are increasingly price‑sensitive but still expect seamless, rapid fulfillment. In the third quarter, the company reported a modest uptick in comparable sales, driven primarily by its “Everyday Low Price” (EDLP) strategy and a surge in grocery and health‑and‑beauty categories, which together offset softer performance in discretionary segments such as apparel and electronics.

Investors will be watching several key metrics for clues about the retailer’s resilience. First, same‑store sales growth in the United States is expected to hover around 2.5% to 3%, a figure that would outpace the broader retail index but still lag behind pre‑pandemic norms. Second, the performance of Walmart’s e‑commerce division—particularly its marketplace and grocery‑delivery services—should reveal whether the company’s heavy investments in technology and logistics are beginning to pay off. Analysts have projected a 7% to 9% rise in online sales, bolstered by the rollout of curbside pickup enhancements and a new subscription model that promises free shipping and exclusive discounts. Third, operating margins are likely to be squeezed by higher transportation and labor costs, a pressure point that Walmart has tried to mitigate through automation in its distribution centers and a renewed focus on private‑label products, which typically carry higher profit margins.

The holiday season will test Walmart’s ability to translate these quarterly gains into sustained momentum. With Black Friday and the broader December shopping window accounting for roughly 15% of the company’s annual revenue, the retailer’s emphasis on value could attract a wave of cost‑conscious shoppers who might otherwise gravitate toward discount chains like Dollar General or online platforms offering deep promotions. However, the competitive environment is intensifying. Amazon continues to expand its grocery footprint through Whole Foods and Prime‑eligible fast‑delivery options, while niche players such as Target are leveraging curated assortments and experiential store formats to lure higher‑spending consumers. Walmart’s response—accelerating its private‑brand portfolio, expanding its “Walmart+” membership, and fine‑tuning its omnichannel inventory—will be critical in determining whether it can maintain market share amid these headwinds.

Beyond the balance sheet, the earnings call is expected to shed light on Walmart’s broader strategic outlook. Chief Executive Doug McMillon has hinted at a “value‑first” narrative for the coming year, suggesting that the company will double down on low‑price assortments while continuing to invest in supply‑chain agility and AI‑driven merchandising. The retailer also plans to roll out a new generation of “store‑within‑a‑store” concepts that blend grocery, health services and digital kiosks, aiming to increase foot traffic and basket size. Moreover, Walmart’s sustainability initiatives—such as reducing food waste and increasing the share of renewable energy in its operations—could become a differentiator for environmentally aware shoppers, though the financial impact of these programs remains to be quantified.

In sum, Thursday’s earnings will provide a barometer of consumer sentiment at a time when the economy teeters between resilience and recessionary pressures. A solid performance could reinforce confidence that Walmart’s value‑centric model remains a bulwark against economic uncertainty, while any miss may signal deeper challenges in converting price‑sensitive traffic into profitable growth. As the holiday shopping season looms, the company’s ability to balance low prices with efficient fulfillment will be pivotal—not only for its own earnings trajectory but also for setting the tone of the broader retail sector in the months ahead.
